n: The psalm opens abruptly, as if mid-thought: God himself laid the foundation of his city, Zion, upon the holy hills of Jerusalem. Its security rests on him, not on walls.
The Lord treasures Zion, the place of his temple, above every other town in Israel. The ‘gates’ stand for the whole city and the people who gather there to worship.

f.g: The towns and homes of Israel, Jacob’s descendants.

n: The psalmist turns to address the city directly. Wonderful promises have been made about Zion — that God would dwell there and draw the nations to it.

f.g: A Hebrew musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning; possibly a pause or a signal to lift the voice.

n: God speaks, listing Israel’s old rivals and neighbors — Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia — and says of each, ‘this one was born there,’ as if counting foreigners among Zion’s own citizens. It is a striking vision of the nations coming to know the Lord.

f.g: Here a poetic name for Egypt (meaning ‘arrogance’ or ‘storm’), not Rahab of Jericho.
Hebrew Cush, the land south of Egypt.

n: People from everywhere will be spoken of as Zion’s children, and the Most High himself will make the city firm. Belonging to Zion becomes a matter of new birth and covenant, not ancestry.

f.w: This and that man was born in her

f.g: Hebrew Elyon, ‘Most High,’ a title of God.

n: The Lord keeps a register of his people, like a census book, and enrolls each as a native of Zion. Scripture often pictures God keeping a book of the names of the faithful.
The psalm ends in celebration: singers and dancers or musicians rejoice in Zion, saying that every source of life and blessing is found in her. Springs of water were precious in a dry land.

f.g: Fountains or sources; figuratively, the origin of all joy and life.
